name: interesting-return-value
intent: Make a routine return the value its caller is expected to act on - the computed result, the previous value, the outcome, or the receiver itself for further calls - so the caller never has to re-derive it and the last line of the method says plainly whether the routine exists for its result or only for its side effect.
problem: A method already knows something the caller needs - the object it just created, the value that was replaced, whether anything actually changed, or a status the caller must check - yet it is declared void (or falls off its end returning None/undefined), so the caller has to ask the same object again (a second query that may observe a different world) or ignore the outcome in silence; and a reader scanning the method cannot tell whether a useful value is produced or the method is used purely for its side effect.
context: Local method design in any language: state-mutating operations on collections and aggregates, builder and configuration steps, lookup operations that can find nothing, I/O primitives that report partial results or failures, and any routine whose result the caller would otherwise have to re-derive. The decision matters most where the language defaults to returning nothing (C, Java, Python, JavaScript) and is most enforceable where the toolchain can mark a result as required (Swift, Rust, Go, C++17+, C23).
benefits: The caller acts on the result in the same step: no follow-up query, no recomputation, and no window in which another statement or another thread changes the state the caller was about to read.
The signature states intent: a value-returning method is visibly a producer and a void/Unit/() method is visibly a procedure, so misuse by a reader - or by static analysis - is visible.
Composition becomes possible: the returned value feeds the next call (builder chains, collection pipelines, tap/also debug steps, stream insertion), keeping call sites short and linear.
Failures travel as values when the return type carries them (status codes, (T, error), Optional, Result), so every call site has to decide what to do about them.
Outcomes become observable and testable: the result of the operation is an ordinary value an assertion can check instead of a hidden side effect on a collaborator.
Where the ecosystem can express it ([[nodiscard]], #[must_use], @discardableResult, CA1806, unused_must_use), forgetting to check a result becomes a warning or a compile error at zero runtime cost.
tradeoffs: Returning a value nobody is expected to use is worse than returning nothing: it invites callers to depend on an incidental value and freezes a representation choice into the public contract.

Must-use enforcement is opt-in, per API and per toolchain: nothing in C, Java, Python or JavaScript stops a caller from discarding a result, so the convention must be re-established for every new method.
Returning the receiver makes a mutation look like a query: setter chains read as expressions, the command/query distinction blurs, and the receiver escapes from methods whose result has no meaning.
Chained calls produce train-wreck statements that are awkward to step through and hide intermediate values; a step that fails in the middle of a chain is hard to attribute.

Value returns cost something in the languages that copy: returning a large object by value (C++), or wrapping every optional result (Optional/Result), adds allocation and moves that a void method never paid.
Mixing channels doubles the contract: a method that both returns a status and throws - or both returns a value and reports failure out of band - forces every caller to read two rulebooks.

participants.responsibility: Computes or observes the outcome and returns it as the method's value - the created object, the previous value, whether anything changed, a status, or the receiver itself - instead of leaving the caller to re-derive it.
Consumes the returned value - continues on the returned object, tests the outcome, records the replaced value - or discards it deliberately and visibly rather than by accident.

The interesting part of the outcome carried as an ordinary value: the computed result, the receiver for chaining, the replaced value, a boolean or enum outcome, or an explicit empty/error result (None, Optional, Result, error, a status code).

use_cases: Collection and aggregate operations that report what happened: Map.put returning the value it replaced, Set.add returning whether the collection changed, pop/remove returning the element it took out.
Builder and configuration APIs where every step returns the receiver so the construction reads as one chain (StringBuilder.append, Kotlin apply/also, Ruby tap, C++ operator<<).

Command handlers and factory methods returning the created entity or its identifier so the caller can route, log or continue without a second lookup (a create endpoint answering 201 with the resource).
Lookup operations that have a real 'nothing' answer: returning Optional/Option/a null object or an explicit found-flag instead of a bare null that propagates silently.
I/O and parsing primitives whose result the caller must act on: a byte count, the consumed length, a status code, or an error value (C's ssize_t plus errno, Go's (n, error), Rust's Result).

State-machine transitions returning the next state or the event that triggered the transition, so the caller can react to the outcome without re-inspecting internal state (common in parsers, network protocol handlers, and UI event systems).

Configuration and validation pipelines where each step returns a validated copy or a list of validation errors, so callers can accumulate and report all problems at once rather than stopping at the first failure (流行的 in form libraries and schema validators).
Cache and memoisation wrappers returning the cached entry or a hit/miss indicator, enabling callers to distinguish 'found value' from 'expensive recomputation not performed' without a second call.

Concurrency primitives returning the result of a completed task or a join handle, so futures/promises can be chained without an extra inspection call (Java CompletableFuture, JS Promise.then, .NET Task<T>).

Python's dict.pop and dict.popitem remove an entry while returning the removed value (or key/value pair), so callers can consume the exact mutation outcome without a second lookup (Python standard library).
JavaScript's Map.prototype.delete returns true only when an entry was removed and false when the key was absent, making an idempotent mutation's outcome directly branchable (MDN Web Docs).

.NET TryParse APIs return a boolean success outcome while exposing the parsed value through an out parameter, avoiding exception-driven control flow for expected invalid input (Boolean.TryParse and Int32.TryParse).
avoid_when: The method is genuinely a procedure and its result would be a meaningless constant (true, this, a fabricated status): return nothing (void/Unit/()) so no reader is invited to check a value that carries no information.
The caller is the next line in the same function and already holds the value: an ordinary local variable or expression is clearer than passing the value out and straight back in.
The value is expensive to produce and usually not needed (a deep copy, a full read-back): offer a separate query method instead of making every mutating call pay for it.
The language already enforces the contract you want (Rust Result, Go error, Swift's default unused-result warning): do not re-wrap it in a custom status convention.
A fluent chain would be built around a type the design never intended as a DSL: plain statements are simpler than making every setter return self.
anti_patterns: Always returning this from every mutator, so side-effecting methods masquerade as queries and call sites become train wrecks.
A return value nobody consumes - a defensive copy, a status flag, a computed summary - where the wasted work is annoying but the misleading signature is the real damage.
Fake interesting values: returning true/OK/success constants that cannot vary, which teaches callers that return values are noise and makes them skip the ones that matter.

Ignoring an error-carrying result because the language allows it (an un-awaited Task, an unchecked write return, a discarded Result, an Optional left unwrapped) - the only signal of failure disappears.
Returning the internal collection, cursor or mutable buffer as the interesting value, so callers can act on representation the object meant to hide.
design_principles: Intention-revealing code: a method's value is part of its contract, so a reader should be able to tell from the last line whether a useful object is produced (Beck's stated rationale for the pattern).
Command-query separation: returning a value marks a method as a computation; a side-effecting command should return nothing rather than blur the two categories.
Single level of abstraction: the value returned by one composed step is what the next step consumes, so composition does not reach back into the object's state.
Encapsulation: return something the caller can act on, not the representation the object holds - the return type is public API and should be chosen like one.
Fail-fast: making failure part of the returned value (or marking the result must-use) forces a decision at the call site instead of at the next crash.
best_practices: Return the value the caller would otherwise have to recompute: the created entity, the replaced value, whether anything changed, or the status of the attempt.
Return the receiver only when the caller's expected next act is another call on that same object; return the real result otherwise.

Make the must-use contract explicit where the ecosystem can express it: [[nodiscard]] (C++17+, C23), #[must_use] (Rust), the default unused-result warning plus @discardableResult (Swift), CA1806 (C#), (T, error) (Go), Optional/Result where null would otherwise mean too many things.
Keep the void case honest and boring: when there is genuinely nothing to report, return nothing and let the type say so (void/Unit/()) instead of a placeholder value.
Name the method after the value it returns, or the change it makes, so callers can tell a producer from a procedure without reading the body.
Discard deliberately and visibly where discarding is legitimate - an explicit (void) cast, let _ =, _ =, a documented ignore - so the next reader sees a decision rather than an oversight.

In languages with algebraic data types, prefer returning Option/Result over null or zero to represent absent or failed outcomes: the type system forces callers to handle the missing-value case, eliminating entire classes of NullPointerException and missing-return-value bugs.

When returning the receiver for chaining, ensure the method is also callable as a standalone statement without pipeline context — avoid a fluent-only interface that forces a chain where a plain statement would be clearer.

For boolean-returning mutators, return whether the state actually changed (the conventional form) rather than always returning true, so repeated calls are observably idempotent and callers can detect no-op cases.

Annotate types that carry a must-use guarantee (Result, Optional, error codes) with the language's dedicated attribute rather than relying on convention alone; a lint-passing annotation is self-documenting API contract that static analysis can enforce.
sources: Kent Beck, Smalltalk Best Practice Patterns (Prentice Hall, 1997) — Formatting chapter, 'Interesting Return Value' (pp. 188-189).

Bertrand Meyer, Object-Oriented Software Construction (Prentice Hall, 1988; 2nd ed. 1997) — introduces Command-Query Separation as the foundational principle: queries return a value, commands perform side effects and should return nothing. This inversion of the Pascal tradition is the theoretical bedrock for the Interesting Return Value pattern.

Kevlin Henney, '97 Things Every Programmer Should Know' (O'Reilly, 2010) — 'Make the Missing Result Meaningful' entry: elaborates on returning meaningful values from operations that could fail, extending the pattern beyond Smalltalk to all mainstream languages where void-returning mutators are the default anti-pattern.

cppreference.com — C++ [[nodiscard]] attribute (C++17, C++20): compilers emit a warning when a nodiscard return value is discarded; C++23 extends this with optional string-literal reason (e.g., [[nodiscard("PURE FUN")]]). Enforced by MSVC /W4, GCC -Wunused-result, and Clang. https://www.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/attributes/nodiscard

The Rust Team, The Rust Programming Language — #[must_use] attribute (stabilised Rust 1.0; expanded to functions in Rust 1.30) triggers the unused_must_use lint at compile time. Standard library types such as Result, Option, and File::write carry implicit #[must_use] so that failing to handle I/O errors is a compile warning, not a runtime surprise. https://doc.rust-lang.org/rust

ISO/IEC 14882:2020 (C++20 Standard) — §9.12.4 'nodiscard attribute': 'If the return value of a function with a nodiscard attribute is discarded, a warning may be produced.' C23 (ISO/IEC 9899:2024) adds [[nodiscard]] to the standard as a vendor extension to mandatory feature. https://open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n3337.pdf

Apple Swift Evolution — SE-0040 'Replace @discardableResult with a more general attribute': @discardableResult (Swift 2.2) allows callers to discard a value without a warning, while the default (without the attribute) produces a compiler error in Debug builds and a warning in Release. https://github.com/apple/swift-evolution/blob/main/proposals/0040-remove-tier-3.md

Martin Fowler, Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code (Addison-Wesley, 1999) — 'Explore Before You Change' and 'Introduce Explaining Variable' reinforce the pattern's intent: name intermediate results so they communicate intent, making return values and temporary variables equally explicative.
